dialogue.t: So, do you think exams like Qudurat and Tahsili genuinely predict who will succeed at university?
It would be somewhat simplistic to claim that they predict success outright. They measure performance on a particular day, under particular pressure.
But surely the universities wouldn't rely on them if they had no predictive value at all?
True. There is a strong case to be made that they correlate with first-year grades, although that correlation seems to fade by the third or fourth year.
Why do you think it fades?
The evidence would seem to suggest that factors like motivation, study habits and even family support matter more once students settle in. A test can't really capture those.
So would you scrap the exams altogether?
Not at all. I'd be inclined to argue that they should be one criterion among several, albeit with certain reservations about how heavily they're weighted at the moment.

words.ex: Anecdotal evidence from a handful of friends hardly constitutes proof.

dialogue.t: Here's a post I found: 'Either we ban TikTok completely, or our teenagers will lose the ability to concentrate.' What do you make of it?
To frame it as either a total ban or a lost generation is a false dichotomy. There are plenty of options in between, such as screen-time limits or digital literacy education.
Another user replied: 'My cousin uses TikTok all day and failed his exams, so the app clearly ruins students.'
There's no causal link between one cousin's app usage and his results. He might have failed for countless other reasons. It's purely anecdotal evidence.
And this one: 'If we let students use AI for homework, soon nobody will be able to write a sentence.'
That argument rests on the assumption that any use of AI inevitably leads to total dependence, which is by no means self-evident. It's a textbook slippery slope.
Last one: 'Young people today don't read anymore.'
That's a sweeping generalization that overlooks the many teenagers who read extensively, often online or in genres older people don't recognise as serious reading.

dialogue.t: You have two minutes. Should Arabic or English be the primary medium of instruction in Saudi universities?
What concerns me most is that we're treating this as a purely practical question, when it is in fact a question of identity.
Go on, but surely English is indispensable for science and research?

It is, and I don't deny that. But rarely do we consider what happens to Arabic when it's excluded from laboratories and lecture halls. Not only does it lose prestige, but it also loses the vocabulary it needs to evolve.
So you'd make Arabic the primary language?
Yes. It is precisely because Arabic has such a rich linguistic heritage that we should equip it for modern science, rather than allow it to erode.
And what about English proficiency?

Under no circumstances should we abandon English; it should be taught rigorously alongside. But only when Arabic is used for serious academic work will it remain a language of knowledge rather than merely of tradition.

dialogue.t: You've read all three opinions. Could you summarize them for me?

Certainly. Whereas Dr Al-Harbi contends that remote learning offers unmatched flexibility, Professor Lewis takes a rather more cautious stance, arguing that it works only for highly self-disciplined learners.
And the third expert?
Dr Mansour is the most critical. She maintains that in-person learning is irreplaceable for social development, particularly for younger students.
Do they agree on anything at all?
Surprisingly, yes. What these views have in common is the belief that the quality of teaching matters far more than the format itself.
So where do you stand?

Taken together, these perspectives point to a hybrid model. On balance, I'm persuaded that remote learning can be highly effective, provided that it's combined with regular face-to-face interaction and proper support for less independent learners.

words.ex: The report glosses over the serious privacy concerns surrounding AI tools.
Fears that AI will replace all teachers are largely unfounded.
AI tutors could democratize access to high-quality support.
Universities are rewriting their policies to protect academic integrity in the age of AI.

dialogue.t: Ladies and gentlemen, I rise to propose the motion that artificial intelligence will do more harm than good to education. It threatens academic integrity and erodes students' ability to think independently.
Madam Chair, I rise to oppose the motion that AI will do more harm than good to education. Allow me to address the central claim that AI destroys independent thinking.
Please do. Students already submit essays they haven't written themselves.

My opponent has conveniently glossed over the fact that plagiarism existed long before AI. Far from destroying critical thinking, the evidence clearly indicates that well-designed AI tools can personalize feedback and push students further.
Yet not every school has the resources to design such tools responsibly.
Which is precisely why AI matters. A student in a remote village with no private tutor can now receive instant, tailored support. AI has the potential to democratize education, not degrade it.
Then I'll leave the house to weigh the risks I've outlined.
In closing, I would urge you to consider that the fears behind this motion are largely unfounded. The question is not whether AI belongs in education, but how wisely we use it. I urge you to oppose.

grammar.title: Rhetorical Contrast with 'Far from'
grammar.ar: تُستخدم العبارة Far from متبوعة باسم أو بفعل منتهٍ بـ ing للتعبير عن أن الحقيقة عكس ما يُدّعى تماماً، أي «بعيداً عن أن يكون... بل على العكس». وهي أداة قوية في المناظرات لرفض ادعاء الخصم وتقديم الحقيقة المضادة في الجملة نفسها. لاحظ أن الجملة الرئيسية بعد الفاصلة تحمل الفكرة المعاكسة، مثل: Far from harming students, AI supports them.
examples: Far from replacing teachers, AI frees them to focus on what matters most.
Far from being a passing trend, generative AI is reshaping assessment worldwide.
Far from solving the problem, the ban has simply driven AI use underground.
